title: Meta’s New Feel-Good AI Ad Uses a Song About the World Ending
gist: Meta ran an Instagram ad insisting AI will not leave people behind, set to David Bowie's 'Five Years' — a song about the world ending — with the apocalyptic opening verse cut; its spokesperson defended the choice with a Bowie quote sourced to a fan site that describes the song as a dystopian nightmare. WIRED places it in a genre of tech reassurance ads alongside Anthropic's and Google's, and FTX's Super Bowl spot nine months before bankruptcy, arguing the ads show these products cannot convince people on their own.

themes.theme: The ad and its song choice

insights.claim: Meta published an ad to its official Instagram account arguing AI will not 'make us less connected' or 'leave us behind', scored to David Bowie's 1972 track 'Five Years', a song about the end of the world.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: The largest consumer AI distributor is now spending brand budget defending AI itself, not a product — a tell on how bad consumer sentiment has gotten.
insights.quote: Call us optimists, call us dreamers, call us whatever the hell you want—but we’re betting on people, and we like those odds
insights.locator: On Thursday morning, Meta published an ad to its official Instagram account

insights.claim: The ad uses only the middle verse of 'Five Years' and skips the opening lines about Earth dying and having five years left to cry in.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: Selective licensing edits are the kind of detail that turns a brand campaign into a news cycle about the brand's judgment.
insights.locator: Perhaps understandably, it skips other parts of the song

insights.claim: Meta's ad takes special care to highlight smart-glasses use cases that are not covert recording of women, an implicit acknowledgment of the product's reputational problem.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: Ad copy that pre-empts a specific abuse case tells you which controversy the company thinks is suppressing adoption.
insights.locator: The ad also takes special care to highlight use cases for its controversial smart glasses

insights.claim: Meta's spokesperson defended the song choice with a 1972 Bowie quote about turning fear of the future into 'a wave of optimism', sourced to the fan site BowieBible.com — the same site that describes the song as a dystopian nightmare of panic and violence.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: Sourcing a corporate defense to a fan site, which then contradicts it, is a reputational own-goal worth noting in how Meta handles press.
insights.locator: When reached for comment, Meta spokesperson Francis Brennan said

insights.claim: Bowie's drummer Mick Woodmansey said in a 2018 interview that the band knew the song was about the end of the world and that Bowie was crying while recording the vocal.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: Corroborating testimony from the recording session forecloses the 'it's actually optimistic' defense.
insights.quote: Well, we chatted about it, and we knew it was about the end of the world and pretty depressing
insights.locator: BowieBible.com also quotes from a 2018 interview with drummer Mick Woodmansey

insights.claim: Warner Chappell Music owns Bowie's catalog and therefore has discretion over where his songs are placed, meaning the estate's wishes are not the gate for AI-brand licensing.
insights.speaker: Jeremy D. Larson, deputy director of Pitchfork
insights.so_what: Catalog ownership, not artist intent, determines AI-era sync licensing — relevant to anyone valuing music catalogs against reputational risk.
insights.locator: He also says that since Warner Chappell Music owns Bowie’s catalog

insights.claim: Stripping songs of context for commercials is a long-standing advertising practice, exemplified by a Carnival Cruise ad using an Iggy Pop song about heroin addiction.
insights.speaker: Jeremy D. Larson, deputy director of Pitchfork
insights.so_what: The precedent argues the backlash is about AI specifically, not about sync licensing norms.
insights.locator: taking songs out of context for commercials is a time-honored tradition

insights.claim: A Pitchfork editor argues using Bowie's work for AI feels 'especially and specifically nonconsensual', a framing that maps artist-consent objections about AI training onto ad licensing.
insights.speaker: Jeremy D. Larson, deputy director of Pitchfork
insights.so_what: Consent is becoming the default critical frame for anything AI touches in music — a structural headwind for AI brand partnerships with catalogs.
insights.quote: Hearing [Bowie’s] work used for AI just feels especially and specifically nonconsensual
insights.locator: “Meta choosing this specific song where the context for human connection is the apocalypse

insights.claim: Tech companies have repeatedly run heavy-handed reassurance ads: Anthropic's 'There's hope in hard questions' opens on a burning building and gravestones before pivoting to optimism, Google's 2024 Gemini ad had a father draft his daughter's fan letter to Sydney McLaughlin-Levrone, and FTX's 2022 Super Bowl Larry David spot told viewers not to miss out.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: A recognizable ad genre marks the point in a technology cycle where public trust, not capability, is the binding constraint on adoption.
insights.locator: Over the past few years, tech companies have made several heavy-handed attempts

insights.claim: FTX filed for bankruptcy roughly nine months after its Super Bowl ad telling viewers not to miss out on crypto and NFTs.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: The cautionary datapoint the piece uses to imply reassurance advertising is a contrarian indicator on the underlying business.
insights.quote: FTX filed for bankruptcy about nine months later.
insights.locator: “Don't be like Larry,” reads the text overlay

insights.claim: The proliferation of goodwill advertising shows tech companies are failing to sell products that on their own convince people they are not making the world worse.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: If the product cannot carry the sentiment, marketing spend rises without fixing churn — watch brand spend as a proxy for weak organic adoption.
insights.quote: many tech companies are failing to sell products that independently convince people that they are not actively making the world worse
insights.locator: Of course, it’s understandable that tech companies would use every tool at their disposal

insights.claim: Mark Zuckerberg framed the campaign as giving every person the tools to reach their full potential and making sure the benefits of technology are distributed to everyone.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: CEO-level framing of AI as distributive rather than disruptive is the positioning Meta will defend against labor and regulatory criticism.
